notes.meaning: Joshua sent two spies in secret from Shittim to scout the land, especially the fortress of Jericho. God had already promised them victory, but Joshua still acted with practical wisdom and careful planning. The spies lodged at the house of a woman named Rahab, where out-of-town visitors would attract less suspicion.

Watchmen quickly alerted the king of Jericho that Israelite spies had entered the city at nightfall. The king immediately sent word to Rahab, ordering her to hand over the strangers. Even though the Canaanites were terrified, their king tried to resist God's plan instead of repenting.

Rahab had already hidden the two spies before the king's messengers arrived. She misled the officers by claiming the men had left at dusk when the gates were closing, and she urged them to give chase quickly. While her brave action protected the spies, Bible teachers note that her lie was still a sin, which God mercifully pardoned because of her genuine faith.

differ.view: Some Baptists note that while Rahab's lie was wrong, it is explained by her pagan background, and God would have protected the spies even without her deception.

notes.meaning: Rahab took the two men up to her flat roof and covered them with stalks of flax that were laid out to dry in the sun. Flax was harvested in early spring and used to make linen cloth. These thick plants made an ideal hiding place where the king's officers would not spot them.

The king's soldiers followed Rahab's false lead and rushed down the road toward the shallow river crossings of the Jordan. As soon as the pursuers marched out, the city gate was locked behind them. This shut the spies inside the city walls, but God was already directing a way for them to escape.

Before the spies lay down to sleep on the roof, Rahab went up to speak with them. She boldly stated that she knew the Lord had given the land to Israel. A terrible dread had fallen upon the whole region, fulfilling God's earlier promise that Canaan would melt with fear before His people.

Rahab told them that Jericho had heard how the Lord dried up the Red Sea forty years earlier and destroyed the powerful Amorite kings east of the Jordan. These miracles crushed the courage of the Canaanites, but they led Rahab to believe that the Lord is the one true God over heaven and earth. Unlike her stubborn neighbors, she surrendered to God's authority.

Rahab asked the spies to swear a sacred oath by the Lord that they would show loyal kindness to her family. Because she had risked her life to protect them, she asked for a reliable pledge that her parents, brothers, sisters, and their households would be saved from death. Her faith showed itself in her deep concern for the rescue of her loved ones.

The spies pledged, 'Our lives for your lives!' They promised to treat her family with kindness and truth when the Lord delivered the land to them, provided she kept their mission secret. Even before the battle began, God's mercy made a place of safety for a foreign woman who put her trust in Him.

Rahab lowered the spies out of her window with a strong rope because her house was built into the outer city wall. She instructed them to hide in the nearby mountain caves for three days until the search party gave up and returned. Her local knowledge gave the men a safe route away from danger.

The men gave Rahab two conditions so they would not be guilty of breaking their oath. She had to tie the bright scarlet cord in the window she used to lower them, and she had to gather all her family members inside her house. Many Christian teachers have seen this red cord as a picture of the blood of Jesus, which shelters believers from judgment just like the Passover blood in Egypt.

The spies explained that anyone who walked out of Rahab's house into the street would be responsible for their own death, leaving Israel free of guilt. Anyone who stayed inside would be fully protected, and the spies would answer for their lives. If Rahab revealed their agreement to others, the men would be completely released from their oath.

Rahab agreed to all their terms, saying, 'Let it be as you say.' She sent the spies away safely and tied the scarlet cord in her window so her home would be marked for deliverance. Her prompt obedience proved that her faith in the Lord was real and active.

The spies followed Rahab's instructions and stayed hidden in the rugged mountain caves for three days. The king's soldiers searched the entire road toward the Jordan River but found nothing. God kept the men safe through Rahab's wise plan and their patient obedience.

The two scouts came down from the mountains, crossed back over the Jordan River, and reported everything to Joshua. They announced with confidence that the Lord had already handed the land over to them, because all the inhabitants were melting in fear. Unlike the fearful spies in Moses' day, these men returned full of faith in God's promises.
